cards.title: Switch Lowering in GCC

depth.text: someone traced how a compiler turns **switch statements** into **jump tables**, **bitsets**, or comparison trees

The article follows GCC’s lowering pass: dense case ranges can become **jump tables**, selected groups can become **bit tests**, and leftovers become a probability-balanced comparison tree. Its jump-table heuristic uses a ratio of 8 for speed and 2 for size.

cards.title: AI, Lean, and the Future of Formal Verification, with Lean Creator Leo de Moura

depth.text: AI is making **formal verification** easier, but humans still need to check **models against the code**

Leo de Moura says AI can write code for stated properties and provide a **proof Lean checks**. He says AI-written proofs have reached **50 million lines**, while Mathlib took 10 years to reach 2.5 million. But AI-made models still need to be **checked against the real code**, and people must decide whether the properties describe what they actually want.
data: Time for Mathlib to reach 2.5 million lines

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters point to formal methods catching incorrect steps; others question whether properties are right, say agents can spin in circles, or claim Lean itself has holes.

comments.text: I think the royal combo is Lean 4/TLA+/etc. plus AI plus a deterministic generator. For large systems formal method assertions need to be compressed down to a human comprehensible size. This can happen when the assertions are confirming the accuracy of a model and its attached code generators. The generator can generate proofs of the generated code and a human only needs to ensure that the…

What do people think of property based testing? I’ve set up a few property based tests and it feels almost like formal verification. I know it’s not the same thing, but PBT’s can catch all sorts of absolutely crazy bugs that I never would think to check for. Stateful stuff, cross-service stuff. My only gripe with PBTs has always been the tedious setup, but LLMs solve that. I haven’t seen much…

> ... But we expect, in the next few months and years, people will focus way more on the specifications, on the models, on the properties you want the software to have. Does anyone have resources on learning modelling for formal verification? (Does not have to be in Lean)
If you use agents to generate formal verification, how do you tell if the properties that are verified are the correct ones?

Currently the foundation theories in mathlib are built with the assumption that formal proofs are expensive. Concepts are fragmented to share as much proof as possible. With LLM the assumption is no longer correct. Concepts and proofs should be built to fit human thinking as much as possible and proofs can be ported by LLMs between theories. Lean would ensure that the translation is correct.

cards.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8

depth.text: a **Linux kernel bug** is **reachable remotely**, before an app sees the connection

CVE-2026-98432 is a **CVSS 9.8** use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake; it can leak kernel memory, corrupt it, or crash the machine. Anthropic says Claude built a **working remote root exploit** for servers with a multipath TCP listener, while Ubuntu and RHEL still had **no fix** as of October 29.

cards.camps: Two camps: the write-up says Anthropic's demonstrated exploit needs an MPTCP listener; some commenters say the bug itself doesn't, and that network filtering or single-core systems may limit exploitation.

comments.text: I've been compiling a list of cybersecurity RSS feeds to build a small automation (with oversight from Hermes agent) to ping me (ntfy.sh or just Telegram) when a CVE requires my intervention (matching them to a list of services I run for clients and myself.) Some notes I've got about this: - MPTCP is not a requirement, it is a generic use-after-free. - Exploitability over the internet is unlikely, most ISP routers drop packets with IP options fields. - At least according to Red Hat, dropping packets with IP options yourself helps, but is not a full mitigation. - Successful exploit requires multiple CPU cores to process packets, so systems with just a…

cards.title: Sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust

depth.text: someone built a **Rust VPN tool** that can move **packet encryption work** to other threads

**sanstun** is a sans-IO Rust implementation of WireGuard. It **separates packet bookkeeping from encryption**, letting a PendingEncapsulate move to another thread; the post says bookkeeping is 2% for a 1280-byte packet and hints at a potential speedup of **more than 45x**, though it says that is hard to achieve in practice.

cards.camps: Two camps: one commenter says rewriting without async can make function coloring worse; another says sans-IO designs are easier to test and can share code between async and blocking IO.

comments.text: It was all going great until I read > The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules. Async is not I/O. It can be used for I/O, but it's just a way of writing pure, deterministic state machines that keeps a logical flow together instead of scattered over a bunch of transitions. Even if you choose to manually compile your async flows into explicit…

Sweet, this is basically how I design my protocol implementations in rust as well. Way more testable, the bulk can be shared between async and blocking IO, it's a lot easier to completely ban unsafe in your dependencies (excepting std and core), etc.
Mullvad spun their own implementation off of boringtun as well (called gotatun[0]) [0] https://github.com/mullvad/gotatun

One of the fundamentally great things about the Wireguard protocol is the simplicity. A small codebase can implement it, and that’s lead to some great libraries and innovation. Another great (and subtle) thing is the monotonically increasing sequence number. Note that it isn’t incrementing, like DTLS. This small thing makes it so much easier to implement with efficient concurrency, and event…

I've recently been developing a VPN Manager implementation using Rust, and the underlying architecture also uses WireGuard. Currently, I'm using WireGuard gotatun developed by Mullvad. I wonder if you've tested any related data, such as performance curves, connection jitter, and so on, as well as things like security implementations.

cards.title: Building an AI-native engineering org

depth.text: FurtherAI used **AI** to **ship code faster**, then gave engineers more say over **what to build**

At FurtherAI, code changes merged per engineer each day grew **about 5x**, while the revert rate stayed under half a percent. AI reviews **99%** of changes before a person does, but planning and review now take 70% of the time, so the team wants **engineers to own more decisions**.
data: Code changes merged per engineer each day
Changes AI reviews before a person

cards.camps: Two camps: some see AI tools and more engineer ownership as a way to move faster; others say speed and code-volume metrics don't prove business value, and warn that less review can hurt quality.

comments.text: Not a single mention of value or revenue. Only three metrics went up: LOC, token spend and presumably release speed/frequency. What's the markup (profit/COGS)? is it up? Customer satisfaction? Is NPS moving one way or another?

To me, true "AI-native" engineering will be one where questions…

That means we are already 6-8 months in, and not far from having a full year of experience of what that actually looks like, albeit weirdly influenced by the increase in model capabilities during that period. I'm looking forward to those retrospectives. Did this turn out…

cards.title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it

depth.text: the ice in Norway is melting and revealing **Stone Age arrows** as ancient **ice patches disappear**

The Secrets of the Ice team found **48 prehistoric arrows** this year; more than **100 arrowheads and arrow shafts** have been recovered from one ice patch over the years. They estimate most ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next **20 years**.

comments.text: Reading the comments on any sort of environment adjacent news on this website is like a form of self torture. You'd think having access to a large corpus of humanity's written knowledge could help, but it seems like it's making it worse.
To be clear, so far some of the oldest ice found is over 6 million years old... https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/six-million-year-old-ice-d...
What's most impressive to me is how razor sharp the slate arrowhead they show in the top photo is. I've seen photos of many stone age arrowheads but they are usually much more dull and blunted.
So this means these areas were once not ice covered? Does this mean the area is returning to what it was a thousand years ago? And, back then, this was the normal or is ice covering the normal?
I'm slightly surprised they're just holding these artefacts with bare hands. I thought that was generally a no-no for dealing with objects untouched for thousands of years

cards.title: GitHub Incident with Actions, Pages, and Webhooks

depth.text: GitHub had an **outage** that delayed **Actions**, Pages deployments, and webhook events before services recovered

Delays affected **Actions workflows**, Pages deployments, and webhook events; errors also affected **code search and live updates**. GitHub said affected services recovered after mitigation, and the incident was resolved.

cards.camps: Two camps: some blame free CI and want it separated from paid infrastructure; others say self-hosting or switching to Forgejo has reduced outages for them.

comments.text: The shape of this HN duplicate detector actually works as a GitHub uptime chart: https://news.ycombinator.com/from?site=githubstatus.com It's driven by aggregated user complaints, so it's pretty high-quality. Comment counts are a proxy for "how bad was the outage" + "how long was the outage thread topical for". edit to add: Here's a scatterplot of the same, https://files.catbox.moe/hhfh4l.png
I think all they have to do is stop giving free CI to everyone and this reliability issue will be solved immediately. Disclaimer: I am building a code forge myself at https://juju.bi
It bugs me how there can be an acknowledged live incident happening today with Actions, and yet down the page where it shows last 30d uptime for actions, today's little rectangle is a chipper green.
Lesson for every infra provider: physically separate your free tier infra from your paid tier infra.
Self-hosted GitHub Actions on AWS spot are still working. After many outages we had to build our own free runner https://github.com/supercorp-ai/superci

cards.title: Show HN: Auto Dismiss Mac OS "Allow <app> to find devices on local networks?"

depth.text: someone made a tool to **auto-dismiss** Mac OS prompts asking apps to find devices on **local networks**

Commenters say the dialog offers no **concrete clue** about what an app is doing. One commenter jokes that the tool is an **unsandboxed, unverified app** requesting Accessibility permissions; others say browsers and games use local-network access for discovery and LAN play.

cards.camps: Two camps: one view says only printer or scanner utilities, media servers, or LAN-discovery tools need it; another says browsers, media players, Spotify, Steam, and LAN games need it too.

comments.text: The big problem with these permission dialogs, is their lack of technical detail about what the app is actually trying to do which triggers them. How do I know whether to say "Allow" or "Disallow" when it gives me no idea what either option actually means in concrete?
Have a problem with pesky permissions dialogs from sandboxed apps? This unsandboxed unverified app that requests Accessibility permissions, to the rescue!
Can I have the opposite, a tool that automatically clicks on "allow"? I installed the app, it's fine.

I'd rather something tell me exactly why this popped up in the first place, as every new OS version seems to introduce more triggers. I have apps that now pop this up when I quit, which doesn't make much sense.
Says a lot about the state of Mac OS.

cards.title: Bunny CDN Security Incident

depth.text: bunny.net pulled a server after its provider reported **unauthorized access**, then began **replacing certificates**

The provider reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software; bunny.net says it cut traffic to its Armenia node within **20 minutes**, preserved security logs, wiped the server and removed it. bunny.net's investigation found **no evidence** the node or its data were accessed, though it cannot rule that out; if access happened, temporarily cached content, Pull Zone configurations and TLS certificates on the server could have been exposed. **Managed certificates** for custom domains are being reissued in controlled batches, with completion expected by the end of October 31.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call Bunny's response prompt and competent; others say wiping the server likely destroyed evidence and reflects a poor incident-response plan.

comments.text: Prompt and competent response, as expected from bunny. "Last week, one of our infrastructure providers reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software. One of our CDN nodes, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by this provider. After receiving the alert from the affected provider, our engineering team took immediate action. Within 20 minutes, we…

Bunny used Gcore in Armenia. Gcore themselves got hacked, not Bunny. Bunny was just an affected downstream, in only one of their POPs. https://lowendtalk.com/discussion/222315/gcore-compromised-v... The title is heavily misleading.

While neither investigation has found any indication of unauthorized access to our server, we cannot completely rule out the possibility.
If unauthorized access to our CDN node did occur, the potentially exposed information would have been: temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations, and TLS certificates stored on that server.

cards.title: Cloudflare Turnstile solver library (no headless browser required)

depth.text: someone built a tool to solve **Cloudflare checks** without a **headless browser**

**cfsolve** returns either a **Turnstile token** or a **cf_clearance cookie**, using a browser profile with recorded responses to Cloudflare’s browser checks. The author reports one user had trouble with European proxies but succeeded with US proxies, possibly because Cloudflare serves different versions by region.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see bypasses as a way around frustrating blocks; others warn that publishing workarounds can fuel escalation and abuse.

"The walls have ears." Personally I would be careful about poking this bear so publicly. All it does is accelerate escalation and cause those of us who have been subjected to user-agent discrimination and found our own workarounds even more difficulty. With the rise of AI, this point may be moot, but this is still a war and anything you make public can and will be used against you.

My Cloudflare solver is command + w. It's 100% reliable in a headful browser and occasionally results in finding an alternative site that doesn't place its priorities (denying bots) over the user's (judicious use of time).
For better or worse, it's like `yt-dlp` — constant race against CF, so it's not reliable. It's probably for better.
